blocks.text: Code mode: make your agents 2x faster and 2x cheaper on long tasks

inlines.text: Code mode: make your agents 2x faster and 2x cheaper on long tasks

blocks.text: Everyone I talk to has an opinion about code mode right now. Mine was lit by Prime Intellect's Prime Agent, a coding harness built around a persistent REPL, and by Alex Zhang's speculative programmatic tool calling, which (among other things) can run tools while the model is still streaming code. Cloudflare has one. Anthropic has one. We've had a few of our own, from MCP code execution to Pydantic Monty. Coding agents are moving the same way: OpenCode 2 now sends MCP tools through Code Mode by default, and Pi ships a codemode tool. The pitch usually goes like this: stop making the model call your tools one at a time, let it write a little program that calls them instead, and everything gets cheaper, faster and better.

blocks.text: I believe that. But almost every number I'd seen came from agents with hundreds of tools or huge payloads, and many agents in the wild are boring: a handful of CRUD tools and a job to do. So I built a benchmark out of exactly that. Five small Pydantic AI apps, single-item tools only, and three kinds of work: everyday requests, long multi-step jobs, and five tasks I could dial from 5 items to 200. Eight models, code mode off and on, 5,276 graded runs on an internal benchmark.

blocks.text: The loop, and why it hurts

inlines.text: The loop, and why it hurts

blocks.text: In a normal tool-calling agent, the model picks a tool, emits some JSON, stops, waits for the harness to run it, reads the result, and picks again. The model sits in the middle of every step, and the costs compound: tool definitions crowd the context, every intermediate result flows through the model, and, the usual story goes, every tool call is another model turn that resends the whole growing context.

inlines.text: In a normal tool-calling agent, the model picks a tool, emits some JSON, stops, waits for the harness to run it, reads the result, and picks again. The model sits in the middle of every step, and the costs compound: tool definitions crowd the context, every intermediate result flows through the model, and, the usual story goes, every tool call is another model turn that resends the whole growing context.

blocks.text: Code mode flips it. The tools become functions inside a sandbox, the model writes one program that loops and branches over them, and only the result comes back. In Pydantic AI Harness that sandbox is Monty, our Python interpreter written in Rust, and the model sees a single run_code tool.

. The cart has 122 lines, a list tool that returns at most 50 per page, and a remove tool that takes one id. 22 lines need to go. Without code mode that's three pages of listing and 22 removes, every one of them chosen by the model. With code mode, it's this:

blocks.text:
import asyncio

items, offset = [], 0
while offset is not None:
    page = await list_items(offset=offset, limit=50)
    items += page["items"]
    offset = page["next_offset"]

pricey = [i for i in items if i["unit_price"] > 50]
await asyncio.gather(*(remove_item(item_id=i["id"]) for i in pricey))
len(pricey)
The model never reads the 100 cheap lines. It doesn't have to remember which ids it already removed. The comparison > 50 is done by Python, not by a language model squinting at a float.

blocks.text: That program is code a model wrote, and something has to run it. What that something lets the code touch is the biggest design decision in code mode.

inlines.text: That program is code a model wrote, and something has to run it. What that something lets the code touch is the biggest design decision in code mode.

blocks.text: Prime Agent makes the open choice. Its model's only tool is a persistent IPython kernel, and the rest of the harness, sub-agents included, lives in that kernel as functions. An IPython kernel is a full Python process: unless something around it says otherwise, the code can import any library, read and write files and open network connections. For a coding assistant on your own machine, that's what you want. It's not something I'd put in a web server and let every user's prompt drive.

blocks.text: Samuel wrote a whole post about this, The code is the graph, and if you build agents you should read it. His argument is that graph libraries rebuild control flow badly: "if is a branch. for is a loop. A function call is an edge", and asyncio.gather is a fan-out and a join. Or in his words about a five-line example: "Fan out, join, branch. That is a graph, and it's also a Python function."

blocks.text: The benchmark is trivial on purpose. Five tiny Pydantic AI apps: a shopping cart, a calendar, a chatroom, a kanban board and an inventory system. Each one has only single-item CRUD tools (list, get, create, update, delete), with paginated lists. No shell, no filesystem, no bulk endpoints. If the agent wants to change 200 things, it has to make 200 calls, or write a loop.

50 tests, ten per app. Single edits, bulk changes, rules with branches, lookups and sums. Without code mode, a run made about 13 tool calls.

"Alex is leaving the team. go through Alex's open tasks (not done) in order of id: if it's urgent or high priority, give it to whoever has the fewest open points at that moment..."

blocks.text: Each app is a Pydantic AI agent. With code mode on, it gets Pydantic AI Harness's CodeMode capability with eager execution, which can start running a complete statement before the model finishes writing the run_code call. With code mode off, the same agent calls the same tools directly. Everything was pinned to one commit, and code mode was flipped with a single setting, so the only difference between arms is code mode itself. The prompts are written the way a person actually types, and every run is graded by a deterministic oracle: the app's end state has to match the expected state exactly (money within a cent), and the reply has to contain the right numbers. No LLM judge.

blocks.text: The failures without code mode are the same kind I saw on the everyday tasks, just more of them: arithmetic and bookkeeping over hundreds of records. In the supplier-price test, 16 of 24 runs without code mode failed, against 1 of 24 with it. Six of those runs, from three different models, reported a stock value of $1,671,683.13. The right answer was $1,671,682.13, and their own end states were worth exactly that. The edits were fine; the sum in the reply was not. Every code mode run that gave a value gave $1,671,682.13.

Output is the slow, expensive part, and it's what the model spends writing out every call and every intermediate value. Input tokens fell 53% too, because fewer results pile up in the context.

blocks.text: On short tasks the input side goes the other way. Code mode's guidance (how run_code works, what's available in the sandbox) adds about 2,600 characters to every request, a flat fee you pay per request no matter how small the job. On the everyday tasks input rose 29% while output fell 37%. At 5 items in the scaling tier total tokens rose 65% to 114%. That flat fee is most of the tax, and on long work it disappears into the savings.

blocks.text: The 50 everyday tests are short: four or five requests and a dozen tool calls each. This is where I started, and where code mode's case is quietest.

inlines.text: The 50 everyday tests are short: four or five requests and a dozen tool calls each. This is where I started, and where code mode's case is quietest.

blocks.text: Across all eight models, code mode was 16% cheaper and 11% faster, and right about as often. The average hides a split. Most of the models were already right 94% to 98% of the time without code mode, and stayed there. gpt-6-luna is the exception, and most of its gain is on questions. In the first batch, twelve of the tests asked for a number ("what's my cart total going to be if dairy is 10% off?"), and gpt-6-luna got 38% of them right without code mode and 88% with it. Without code mode the models added up 30 to 120 rows in their heads and missed, stopped after two of three pages, or just declined: "I can't reliably calculate the total from this many cart lines." In the other direction, muse-spark-1.3-contributor was right less often with code mode, and every one of those misses left the app in the wrong state.

blocks.text: Aggregates (questions over many rows) are where code mode shines: 90% to 98% correct, 27% cheaper, 26% faster. Then there's the control group, five tests that are a single operation ("change the sourdough to 2 please"). There code mode cost 8% more and took 16% longer, because the model paid for the guidance and wrote a program to make one call. Bulk edits were cheaper too, but less often right (95% to 90%), and the Muse models account for most of that drop. Categories have 5 to 10 tests each, too few for intervals, so treat those bars as direction.

At 5 items, code mode cost more on three of the five scaling tasks; by 20 it was cheaper on three and level on one. Chat triage crossed over last: it cost more at 5 and 20 messages and only got cheaper from 100. Telling a refund request from other messages means reading the text, so with code mode the messages still pass through the model.
Small models that write buggy code.
gpt-6-luna paid 19% more on the everyday tasks, with 0.56 failed
snippets per run, and every failure is another round trip. Per correct run it still came out cheaper: $0.00121 against $0.00130. On the inventory scaling task its cost grew
with code mode than without, while it got 9 of 15 runs right instead of 3.
Models that print the data back.

muse-spark-1.3-contributor's code mode runs printed much of the data into the conversation, so at 200 items its tokens fell only 5% to 64%. For muse-wonder-1.0-contributor and deepseek-v4.1-flash they fell 57% to 99%.
A snippet that fails halfway and gets rerun can do its first half twice. Three of gpt-6-luna's failures in the long tier created the same records twice.
It can still get things wrong.

On the everyday tasks, muse-spark-1.3-contributor was right 92% of the time with code mode and 98% without, the one drop whose interval clears zero. Most of its misses were bulk edits that left the app in the wrong state. In the scaling tier, two cells went the wrong way, both within noise. In calendar invites at N = 20 (92% → 83%), gpt-6-luna left invites unanswered and claude-haiku-5-5 miscounted its own work. In inventory at N = 5 (100% → 92%), claude-haiku-5-5 twice left a required number out of its reply.

blocks.text: So code mode earns its keep once the data or the task grows past what plain tool calling handles well. On these apps, for most tasks, that point was somewhere between 20 and 50 items.

blocks.text: So why is it the future?

inlines.text: So why is it the future?

blocks.text: Because the curve is real, and it points one way. Code mode charges a flat fee: a couple of thousand characters of guidance per request. Tool calling charges per item: every call written out, every result read back in, every running total held in the model's head. On a single edit the flat fee loses. A few dozen items in, it starts winning, and by 200 items it's not close. I expect agent tasks to keep getting longer. I haven't measured that, but if they do, more and more of them will land on the right side of that curve.

blocks.text: Code mode is also just where the models are heading: writing code looks like the skill they're improving at fastest. My guess is that's because code is checkable, which makes it easy to train on. Either way, giving the model a programming language to drive your tools plays to the strength that's improving fastest.

blocks.text: It also has to be safe to run. Every result above came from code mode inside a sandbox that could reach these apps' tools, an in-memory filesystem and environment, and the clock, and nothing else: no host files and no network. That's the setup we built Monty for.

blocks.text: The next step is the same idea one level up. In dynamic workflows, the functions in the sandbox are sub-agents instead of tools, and the program the model writes is the orchestration. Samuel's graph, written by the model, at runtime, with agents as the nodes. That's the future I mean.

blocks.text: Pydantic AI Harness's CodeMode also has speculative execution: the speculative programmatic tool calling from the top of this post, which starts calls to tools you've declared safe to run early while the model is still writing the run_code call. None of these apps' tools were declared for it, so speculation had nothing to start early. In the first everyday batch it differed from plain code mode only in its longer guidance, and it showed: +7.7 points of success instead of +10.3, and +4% cost instead of -2%. The later batches skipped it. That's not a test of speculation, so I'm not drawing conclusions from it.
